questions.q: What is a site-to-site VPN, fundamentally?
options: An encrypted IPsec tunnel over the public internet connecting an entire on-prem network to a cloud VNet or VPC
A private physical circuit that never touches the public internet
A connection that links two cloud VNets over the provider's own backbone
A VPN client installed on a single remote laptop
questions.explain: Site-to-site VPN connects whole networks together using an encrypted IPsec tunnel that crosses the public internet, unlike a dedicated circuit or VNet peering.

questions.q: How does a site-to-site VPN fundamentally differ from VNet-to-VNet peering?
options: Peering connects two cloud networks over the provider's backbone; site-to-site VPN connects an on-prem network to the cloud over the public internet
They are the same technology with different names in Azure vs. AWS
Peering requires IPsec encryption and site-to-site VPN does not
Site-to-site VPN only works within a single cloud region, while peering works across regions
questions.explain: Peering never touches the public internet because both sides are already in the cloud; site-to-site VPN exists specifically because the on-prem side isn't.

questions.q: In Azure, what resource describes the on-prem side of a site-to-site VPN connection — its public IP and address ranges?
options: The Local Network Gateway
The VNet peering link
The Azure VPN Gateway
The GatewaySubnet
questions.explain: The Local Network Gateway represents the on-prem network: its public IP and the address ranges behind it. The VPN Gateway is the cloud-side resource.

questions.q: What is the AWS equivalent of Azure's Local Network Gateway?
options: The Customer Gateway (CGW)
The Virtual Private Gateway (VGW)
The Internet Gateway
The NAT Gateway
questions.explain: The Customer Gateway describes the on-prem device; the Virtual Private Gateway is the cloud-side resource attached to the VPC.

questions.q: Why do Azure and AWS both provision a site-to-site VPN connection as two tunnels by default?
options: So one tunnel can fail (e.g. a provider-side maintenance event) without taking down the whole connection
Because a single tunnel is not permitted by either cloud provider
To double the available bandwidth automatically with no configuration
Because IPsec requires exactly two tunnels to function at all
questions.explain: The two tunnels terminate on different physical endpoints, giving redundancy if one goes down; the on-prem device must be configured to fail over between them.
